title: Most Profitable Set of Gigs
statement:
A freelancer is offered n gigs. Gig i runs from time start[i] to time end[i] and pays pay[i]. They can work on only one gig at a time, and a gig must be done completely or not at all.

A gig that ends at time t does not clash with one that starts at time t. Return the largest total pay from a set of gigs with no overlaps. The gigs are not given in any particular order.

examples.why: Take [2, 6) for 50 and [6, 9) for 25. Picking gigs by earliest end gives [1, 4) and [4, 7) for only 40.
All three gigs overlap at time 1, so only one can be taken: the best-paid one.
Each gig ends exactly when the next starts, which is allowed, so all three fit.

hints: Greedy rules (earliest end, highest pay) all fail on some input. Think in terms of a choice per gig: take it or skip it.
Sort the gigs by end time. Let best[i] be the most you can earn using only the first i gigs. If you take gig i, what is the latest earlier gig you can combine it with?
best[i] = max(best[i − 1], pay[i] + best[j]), where j counts the gigs whose end ≤ start of gig i. Because ends are sorted, find j with binary search.

explain.intuition:
Each gig is a yes/no decision, and the decisions interact only through time. Sort the gigs by end time. Then for the i-th gig there are two cases. Skip it, and the best total is whatever the first i − 1 gigs could earn. Take it, and you earn its pay plus the best total from gigs that end no later than it starts.

Those earlier compatible gigs form a prefix of the sorted list, because ends are sorted. So "the best total from compatible gigs" is just a DP value at one index, and binary search over the end times finds that index in O(log n). That is the same idea as the weighted version of picking non-overlapping meetings.
steps: Build the list of gigs and sort it by end time.
Let best[0] = 0; best[i] is the answer using the first i gigs in that order.
For gig i (1-based), binary-search the number j of gigs whose end is ≤ its start.
pitfalls: Using a strict < when comparing an end with a start. Gigs that touch are allowed, so the test is end ≤ start.
Sorting by start time and then searching by end time. The prefix property only holds for the order you search in.
Choosing greedily by earliest end, which is right for counting gigs but wrong for maximising pay, as the first example shows.

solutions.title: DP with a linear scan back
solutions.idea: Sort by end. For each gig, scan all earlier gigs for the best compatible total.

solutions.title: DP with binary search
solutions.idea: Sort by end. The gigs compatible with gig i form a prefix of that order, so binary search finds where it ends.

followups: Also return which gigs to take, not just the total. What do you store to walk the choices back?
The freelancer can now work on two gigs at once. How does the state grow?
